newsitem.title: USA: Analysts see 1997 U.S. beef output up over 1996.
newsitem.headline: Analysts see 1997 U.S. beef output up over 1996.

text.p: U.S. beef production in 1997 will likely rise by about one percent compared to 1996, a leading livestock market research group told an industry conference on Saturday.
Topper Thorpe, executive vice president of the market research and analysis service Cattle-Fax, also said prices on all classes of cattle in 1997 were expected to be above their year-ago averages.
"We are past the toughest part of the cattle cycle," Thorpe told the National Cattlemen's Beef Association's convention.
Thorpe said lower cattle prices were giving way to stable- to higher-trending market prices and improved returns for cattle feeders and stocker operators.

"The shrinking cow herd, which could end up by the turn of the century at or below 1990 levels, means there will be fewer calves, declining feeder cattle supplies and less beef the next several years. Normally, this results in higher cattle prices and a return to profitability for all segments," Thorpe said.
In a statement released Saturday, Cattle-Fax said projected Choice fed-cattle prices would average between $64 and $65 per hundredweight (cwt) during 1997.
The price for 750-pound steers should be $65 to $67 per cwt on average, Cattle-Fax said.

Calf prices were expected to average $5 to $7 per cwt above year-ago levels of about $70 per cwt for 500-pound steer calves. Calf prices will likely be higher during the fall months than the annual average, Cattle-Fax said.

Cattle-Fax said the forecast assumed that corn production would be adequate in 1997, and it warned that substantial cattle price variation was likely during the year. Prices were expected to follow more normal seasonal patterns than they did in 1996, but will vary based on region and quality.

Beef output was projected to reach a cycle peak in 1997, but should not increase much more than one percent compared to 1996, Cattle-Fax said. Sizeable reductions in annual beef production were expected in 1999 and 2000.

Per capita beef supplies should be modestly lower in 1997 compared to 1996. Exports of beef and veal will likely exceed total imports, making the U.S. a net exporter of beef on a volume basis for the first time.
The sideways trend in U.S. consumer spending on beef was projected to continue in 1997, but should recover with modest growth from 1998 to 2000, Cattle-Fax said.
U.S. consumers spent approximately $45.5 billion on beef in 1996. That was one percent less than in 1995 and slightly less than the 1991-1995 annual average.

Cattle-Fax said U.S. beef exports were expected to post a 10 to 20 percent volume gain in 1997 compared to 1996. Growth in U.S. exports slowed during the second half of 1996 as foreign buyers reduced purchases in response to perceived food safety concerns.

Grain prices, which are critical factors in shaping the cattle outlook, should remain significantly lower in 1997 compared to 1996, Cattle-Fax said. Corn prices, basis Omaha, Nebraska, were expected to spend most of 1997 trading between $2.25 and $3.00 per bushel.
Based in Englewood, Colorado, Cattle-Fax is a member-owned research and analysis organization serving cattle operators in all segments of the industry.
